summary: Specifies a Telnet profile to support VIP terminal emulation, so applications on BULL hosts can be reached over a TCP/IP network. It is informational and describes a vendor-specific protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: Some old company computers expected a special kind of terminal. This note explains how to pretend to be that terminal over the Internet.

questions: how to emulate bull vip terminals over telnet
how do you emulate bull terminals over telnet
how does tnvip handle screen and printer data
subtitle: Extending Telnet to emulate special-purpose terminal types over TCP/IP networks.

tldr.problem: BULL mainframe systems used block-mode VIP terminals with special capabilities like screen and printer management that standard Telnet could not emulate.
tldr.mechanism: TNVIP extends Telnet with negotiated options (terminal type, end-of-record, binary transmission) and defines a message format with address and command fields to route screen and printer data through a Telnet connection.
tldr.outcome: Informational protocol that enabled BULL terminal emulation over TCP/IP networks before being superseded by more modern terminal solutions.

today: RFC 1921 is an Informational document that has not been updated or obsoleted. It remains a historical record of the TNVIP protocol used by BULL systems in DSA (Distributed Systems Architecture) networks, but modern terminal solutions have superseded it.

sections.title: VIP Terminal Emulation Over Telnet
sections.content:
TNVIP (Telnet VIP) is a Telnet profile that allows emulating BULL VIP (Visual Information Projection) terminals over a TCP/IP network. Unlike the standard Network Virtual Terminal (NVT) that Telnet normally uses, VIP terminals operate in block mode, send and receive data in structured messages, and manage both a screen and an optional attached printer.

The protocol extends standard Telnet by negotiating special options and defining a message format that carries terminal control data, screen updates, printer commands, and status responses. This allows terminal emulation programs on one machine to connect to BULL host applications on another machine via a Telnet connection.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of sending characters one at a time like normal terminals do, these fancy BULL computers send whole blocks of information at once. The TNVIP protocol lets your computer talk to them by adding special rules on top of Telnet to handle those big blocks.

sections.title: Telnet Options and Message Structure
sections.content:
TNVIP requires four Telnet options to be negotiated between the client and server:

  • Terminal Type: Identifies the VIP terminal model (such as VIP7700, VIP7804, or DKU7005) and optionally a mailbox name to request a specific access point on the server.
  • End of Record (EOR): Marks the boundary of each TNVIP message, since the protocol works with block-oriented data rather than individual characters.
  • Binary Transmission: Optional, used when the terminal supports 8-bit binary characters instead of 7-bit ASCII.
  • Suppress Go Ahead: Optional, suppresses Telnet flow control signals so data transmission is synchronized differently.

Each TNVIP message consists of a 2-byte header (address and command fields), optional parameters, and ends with a Telnet EOR code. The address field identifies which device (screen, printer, or screen-copy-printing) the message targets.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the fancy computer and your computer talk, they agree on some rules about how to split up messages and what kind of terminal you're pretending to be. Then every message has a little label saying what it's for and what you want to do.

sections.title: Message Addressing and Commands
sections.content:
TNVIP defines three device addresses in the message header:

  • Screen (0x60): For screen data, terminal type negotiation, local/online state changes, and screen status responses.
  • Printer (0x68): For printer data and printer status messages. Support is optional.
  • Screen Copy Printing (0x69): For printing a copy of the screen contents.

The command byte encodes both a command type (0-31) and a message type: indication (no response expected), request (response required), response (answers a request), or response-and-request (both)). Response messages include ACK (success), ERROR, BUSY, and others like PROTOCOL-VIOLATION or UNKNOWN-COMMAND to handle errors and flow control.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message says where it's going (to the screen, printer, or copy function) and what kind of message it is. Some messages ask for a response back, some just tell you something happened, and some messages say 'this went wrong' if something breaks.

sections.title: Terminal States and Data Flow
sections.content:
The TNVIP client terminal has two main states: LOCAL and ONLINE. In LOCAL state, the terminal can perform local tests or change configuration, and data from the server is suspended. The client sends a LOCAL-STATE request message to the server before switching to local mode, and the server acknowledges and pauses sending screen and printer data until an ONLINE-STATE indication resumes the flow.

When receiving data, the terminal routes messages to the screen or printer buffer based on the address field. If the terminal is in LOCAL state or busy, it returns a BUSY response. For the screen, data messages include two function codes and an STX introducer followed by screen data in the terminal's presentation format (P200 or 7800). The printer can receive data in two modes: formatted print (using terminal presentation commands) or transparent print (raw printer data).
sections.plainLanguage: The fancy terminal can take a break and switch into local mode to run tests, then tell the computer 'I'm back online now.' When data arrives, it checks where it's supposed to go and whether it's busy. If it gets data while it's already printing, it says 'I'm busy, ask me later.'

sections.title: Server-Side Architecture
sections.content:
On the server side, a VIP Terminal Manager (TM) acts as a gateway between the TNVIP connection and the host application. The Terminal Manager presents terminal stations (SN objects) as the logical representation of physical terminal units (TU objects), and logical devices (LD objects) as the logical representation of actual screen and printer devices.

This architecture allows flexible mapping: a single terminal unit can appear as a generic access point (unnamed), or the server can support multiple named mailbox access points that route connections to different physical terminals or logical combinations of devices. For example, one mailbox might route to a terminal's screen while another routes to its printer, or a mailbox might combine a screen from one terminal with a printer from another for presentation to the host application.
sections.plainLanguage: The server on the other end organizes the terminals it manages in a neat way so that when your emulated terminal connects, it can ask for a specific one by name, or just get a default one if it doesn't care.
